newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU leaders tell Europe to prepare for euro.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders tell Europe to prepare for euro.

text.p: European Union leaders made major strides towards monetary union at a two-day summit and urged the region's people, markets and governments to prepare for the launch of the euro single currency in 1999.

After breaking a Franco-German deadlock over a pact to enforce budget discipline within economic and monetary union (EMU), the leaders ended their summit on Saturday determined to put the project on an irreversible course towards completion.
Speaking at a final news conference, French President Jacques Chirac said, "The euro is now credible thanks to a pact for stability and growth which underpins our common currency"
"We've made the euro an instrument for growth and employment," he added.
In their final communique, EU heads of state emphasised how much work they have already done to harden up their plans for EMU.
"The European Council welcomes the further decisive progress which has been made in the preparations for EMU, which will begin on 1 January 1999," the communique said.
It urged "institutions, public authorities and economic agents to intensify their preparations for the starting date."

The leaders called for the rapid adoption of regulations on converting national currencies into euros, which will help businesses to get on with the major overhaul of their information technology systems needed to accommodate the single currency.
They endorsed a new exchange rate mechanism, dubbed ERM 2, that will link the euro with EU currencies which are left outside EMU.
But while basking in the glow of their success, EU leaders also recognised the doubts and fears of many of their citizens about giving up their national currencies.

They underscored the "need to make the euro tangible for citizens," and welcomed Friday's unveiling of the euro bank notes commissioned by the European Monetary Institute, the Frankfurt-based forerunner to a European Central Bank.
They charged the European Commission, the EU's executive, with arranging a design competition for euro coins, with a choice expected during the first half of next year.
Public support for a common currency has been patchy at best, particularly in Germany where opinion polls show consistently strong resistance to the euro.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, acknowledging the fears of his countrymen, told a news conference: "I am sure the majority of the German population think that they are paying a high price," for a single European currency.
"But they will be prepared to live with that if they know that as a result Europe can live in peace."
The communique also called attention to the EU's high rate of joblessness and stressed the need for a more comprehensive strategy to spur employment.
"The fight against unemployment is the priority task of the Union and its member states," the draft said.
The group adopted a declaration recommending measures to spur jobs growth, including a greater focus on labour market reform.

With nearly 18 million out of work in the EU -- and many government critics linking job losses to state austerity programmes needed to qualify for EMU -- EU leaders are well aware just how urgently more jobs are needed.
